chunks: A man called ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ayyūb narrated to me. He said: Abū ʿAmr al-Mutaṭabbib narrated to me. He said: I presented this narration to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام. And ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated from his father, from Ibn Faḍḍāl, and Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, all from al-Riḍā عليه السلام, who said: We presented the book to him, and he said: “Yes, it is true, and Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام used to command his officials according to it.”

He said: “He عليه السلام gave a stated legal assessment for every bone containing marrow when it is broken and then heals without deformity or defect. He divided the prescribed blood-money into six parts, and assigned for the spirit, the fetus, the eyelids, paralysis, the limbs, and the thumb, six prescribed shares for each part. He set the blood-money of the fetus at one hundred dinars, and made the semen of the man up until it becomes a fetus five stages. If it is a fetus before the spirit enters it, it is one hundred dinars. For the drop of fluid he assigned twenty dinars—when a man is startled away from his bride and emits the drop without intending it, Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام fixed twenty dinars in it, one-fifth. For the clot he assigned two-fifths of that, forty dinars; and likewise for a woman if she is struck or attacked and miscarries it. Then for the lump of flesh, sixty dinars, if the woman miscarries it in such a case. Then for the bone, eighty dinars, if the woman miscarries it. Then for the fetus also, one hundred dinars, if an enemy attacks them and the women miscarry in such a case; he imposed that upon the women from the side of the collective indemnity likewise. If the child is born and cries out—meaning the crying—and then they attack by night and kill the children, then for them there is one thousand dinars for the male, and for the female according to this same reckoning, five hundred dinars. As for the woman, if she is killed while carrying a full-term pregnancy and she does not cast out her child, and it is not known whether it is male or female, and it is not known whether it died after her or before her, then its blood-money is two halves: half the blood-money of a male and half the blood-money of a female; and then the blood-money of the woman is complete after that. He also gave a ruling concerning the semen of a man who is startled away from his bride and withdraws the fluid from her without intending that: half of one-fifth of the hundred from the blood-money of the fetus, ten dinars; and if he discharges into her, twenty dinars. He assigned retaliation and indemnity for its wounds according to its blood-money, which is one hundred dinars, and ruled regarding the blood-money of fetal injury according to the reckoning of the hundred, in accordance with what applies to the wounds of a man and a woman in full.”

“He عليه السلام also gave a ruling regarding the body and made it six prescribed divisions: life, sight, hearing, speech, intellect, and loss of voice through nasalization and hoarseness, and paralysis in the two hands and two feet. He set this by analogy to that ruling. Then with each of these he assigned qasāmah according to the extent of the blood-money involved. In qasāmah for life, he set fifty men for intentional killing, and twenty-five men for mistaken killing, corresponding to a blood-money of one thousand dinars. For wounds, qasāmah is by six persons, and what is less than that is calculated upon six persons. Qasāmah applies in life, hearing, sight, intellect, voice lost through nasalization and hoarseness, and deficiency of the hands and feet; these are the six parts of a man. The blood-money for life is one thousand dinars; for the nose, one thousand dinars; for complete loss of the light of both eyes, one thousand dinars; for hoarseness, one thousand dinars; for paralysis of the two hands, one thousand dinars; for the two feet, one thousand dinars; for complete loss of hearing, one thousand dinars; for the two lips when entirely removed, one thousand dinars; for the back when it becomes hunched, one thousand dinars; for the male organ, one thousand dinars; for the tongue when entirely removed, one thousand dinars; and for the two testicles, one thousand dinars. He عليه السلام set blood-money for injuries in all limbs of the head, face, and the rest of the body, including hearing, sight, voice, intellect, the two hands, and the two feet, in cases of severing, fracture, fissure, crushing, exposing bone, drawing blood, displacement of bones, and perforating wounds. Any bone that is broken and heals without deformity or defect, and whose bones are not displaced, has a known blood-money. If the bone is exposed but the bones are not displaced, then there is the blood-money of its fracture and the blood-money of its exposing wound. For every known broken bone, the blood-money for displacing its bones is half of the blood-money of its fracture, and the blood-money for its exposing wound is one quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, for those parts covered by clothing, except the two bones of the forearm and the fingers. For an ulcer that does not heal, there is one third of the blood-money of that limb in which it occurs.”

“If a man is injured in one of his eyes, it is measured by an egg tied over the injured eye, and the extent of the sight of his sound eye is observed. Then his sound eye is covered, and the extent of the sight of his injured eye is observed, and he is given his blood-money according to that calculation. Along with that, qasāmah applies from these six parts, by six persons, in proportion to the injury to his eye. If it is one-sixth of his sight, the man alone swears and is given it. If it is one-third of his sight, he swears and another man swears with him. If it is half of his sight, he swears and two men swear with him. If it is two-thirds of his sight, he swears and three men swear with him. If it is four-fifths of his sight, he swears and four men swear with him. If it is all of his sight, he swears and five men swear with him. That is in qasāmah concerning the two eyes.”

He said: “He عليه السلام also gave a ruling about one who has no one to swear with him, and whose claim about the loss of his sight is not fully relied upon: the oath is multiplied for him. If it is one-sixth of his sight, he swears once; if it is one-third, he swears twice; if it is half, he swears three times; if it is two-thirds, he swears four times; if it is five-sixths, he swears five times; and if it is all of his sight, he swears six times, then he is given it. If he refuses to swear, he is given only for what he has sworn to and what has been trusted from him as truthful. The governor seeks assistance in that through questioning, observation, and verification in retaliation, punishments, and retribution. If something affects his hearing, then similarly something is struck for him so that the limit of his hearing may be known, then that is measured, and qasāmah is according to the extent of the loss of his hearing; if it is all of his hearing, then it is likewise. If wickedness is feared from him, he is left until he becomes heedless, then he is called out to; if he hears, the litigants return him to the judge, and the judge acts regarding him by his judgment and reduces some of what he had taken. If the deficiency is in the thigh or in the upper arm, it is measured with a string: his sound leg is measured, then the injured one is measured by it, and what has diminished from his hand or his leg is known. And if the shin or the forearm is injured from the thigh or the upper arm, it is measured, and the judge considers the extent of his thigh.”

“He عليه السلام ruled regarding the temple of a man: if it is injured and he cannot turn except by twisting himself, then there is half the blood-money, five hundred dinars; and whatever is less than that is according to its proportion. He ruled regarding the upper eyelid: if it is injured and torn, its blood-money is one-third of the blood-money of the eye, one hundred sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar. If the lower eyelid is injured, its blood-money is half the blood-money of the eye, two hundred fifty dinars. If the eyebrow is injured and all its hair is lost, its blood-money is half the blood-money of the eye, two hundred fifty dinars; and whatever part of it is injured is according to that proportion. If the tip of the nose is cut, its blood-money is five hundred dinars, half the blood-money. If a piercing wound is made in it that does not close, by an arrow or a spear, its blood-money is three hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third; but if it is a piercing wound that heals and closes, its blood-money is one-fifth of the blood-money of the tip of the nose, one hundred dinars, and whatever is injured is according to that proportion. If the piercing wound is in one nostril up to the septum, which is the barrier between the two nostrils, its blood-money is one-tenth of the blood-money of the tip of the nose, because that is half, and the septum between the nostrils is fifty dinars. If the shot penetrates one nostril and the septum to the other nostril, its blood-money is sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar. If the upper lip is cut off entirely, its blood-money is half the blood-money, five hundred dinars, and whatever part of it is cut is according to that proportion. If it is split so that the teeth appear, then treated and it heals and joins, then there is the blood-money of its wound, and the assessed amount in it is one-fifth of the blood-money of the lip, one hundred dinars, and whatever part is cut is according to that proportion. If it is torn and disfigured with an ugly deformity, its blood-money is one hundred sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar. The blood-money of the lower lip, if it is cut off and entirely removed, is two-thirds of the full blood-money: six hundred sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar; whatever part is cut is according to that proportion. If it is split until the teeth appear, then heals and joins, it is one hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. If it is injured and severely disfigured, its blood-money is three hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar, and that is one-third of its blood-money.”

He said: I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about that, and he said: “It has reached us that Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام gave it preference because it holds food and water; for that reason he gave it preference in his judgment.” “As for the cheek: if there is a penetrating wound in it and the cavity of the mouth appears through it, its blood-money is one hundred dinars. If it is treated and heals and closes, but a clear mark and severe disfigurement remain, its blood-money is fifty dinars. If there is a penetrating wound through both cheeks, its blood-money is one hundred dinars, and that is half of the blood-money of the one through which the mouth appeared. If it is struck by a blade that penetrates the bone until it reaches the palate, its blood-money is one hundred fifty dinars, of which fifty dinars are assigned for exposing the bone. If it is a perforating wound that does not fully penetrate, its blood-money is one hundred dinars. If it is an exposing wound in any part of the face, its blood-money is fifty dinars. If there is disfigurement in it, the blood-money of its disfigurement is one quarter of the blood-money of its exposing wound. If it is a wound that does not expose the bone and then heals, but there remains a trace in the cheeks, its blood-money is ten dinars. If there is a fissure in the face, its blood-money is eighty dinars. If a piece of flesh falls from it and it does not expose the bone, and it is the size of a dirham or more, its blood-money is thirty dinars. The blood-money of a head wound, if it is exposing, is forty dinars when it is in the body, and in the place of the head it is fifty dinars. If the bones are displaced from it, its blood-money is one hundred fifty dinars. If it is a perforating wound in the head, then that is called al-maʾmūmah, and in it there is one-third of the blood-money: three hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar.”

“He عليه السلام assigned for the teeth fifty dinars for each tooth, and made the teeth equal. Before that, he used to assign fifty dinars for the central incisor, forty dinars for the lateral incisor, thirty dinars for the canine, and twenty-five dinars for the molar. If the tooth turns black for a year and does not fall out, its blood-money is that of a fallen tooth, fifty dinars. If it is cracked and does not fall out, its blood-money is twenty-five dinars. Whatever part of it is broken is according to its proportion from the fifty. If it then falls while blackened, its blood-money is twelve and a half dinars, and whatever part is broken from it is according to its proportion from twenty-five dinars. For the collarbone, if it is broken and heals without deformity or defect, there are forty dinars. If it is fissured, its blood-money is four-fifths of the blood-money of its fracture, thirty-two dinars. If it exposes bone, its blood-money is twenty-five dinars, and that is five parts of its blood-money when broken. If its bones are displaced, its blood-money is half the blood-money of its fracture, twenty dinars. If it is perforated, its blood-money is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, ten dinars. The blood-money of the shoulder, if broken, is one-fifth of the blood-money of the hand, one hundred dinars. If there is a fissure in the shoulder, its blood-money is four-fifths of the blood-money of its fracture, eighty dinars. If the bone is exposed, its blood-money is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars. If the bones are displaced from it, its blood-money is one hundred seventy-five dinars, of which one hundred are for the fracture, fifty for displacement of bones, and twenty-five for the exposing wound. If it is perforating, its blood-money is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars. If it is crushed and heals with deformity, its blood-money is one-third of the blood-money of life: three hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. If it is dislocated, its blood-money is thirty dinars. For the upper arm, if broken and healed without deformity or defect, its blood-money is one-fifth of the blood-money of the hand, one hundred dinars. The blood-money for exposing its bone is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars; for displacement of its bones, half the blood-money of its fracture, fifty dinars; and for perforation, one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars. For the elbow, if broken and healed without deformity or defect, its blood-money is one hundred dinars, and that is one-fifth of the blood-money of the hand. If it is fissured, its blood-money is four-fifths of the blood-money of its fracture, eighty dinars. If it exposes bone, its blood-money is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars. If its bones are displaced, its blood-money is one hundred seventy-five dinars: one hundred for the fracture, fifty for displacement of the bones, and twenty-five for the exposing wound. If there is a perforating wound in it, its blood-money is one-quarter of the blood-money of its fracture, twenty-five dinars. If the elbow is crushed and heals with deformity, its blood-money is one-third of the blood-money of life: three hundred thirty-three dinars and one-third of a dinar. If it is dislocated, its blood-money is thirty dinars. The other elbow is exactly the same.”

“He عليه السلام ruled that there is no retaliation against a father for a man whom his father injures in a matter for which he reproaches him, such that he is left with a defect by cutting or otherwise; rather, he is entitled to blood-money, and retaliation is not carried out. Nor is there retaliation for a woman injured and left defective by her husband; the liability for the defect is upon her husband, and there is no retaliation against him. He عليه السلام ruled regarding a woman with whom her husband had intercourse and caused ifḍāʾ in her, that she is entitled to half her blood-money, two hundred fifty dinars. He عليه السلام ruled regarding a man who ruptured a slave-girl with his finger and tore her bladder so that she could not control her urine, assigning her one-third of the blood-money, one hundred sixty-six dinars and two-thirds of a dinar. And he عليه السلام ruled that she was also entitled from him to her dower according to the women of her people.” And in the narration of Hishām ibn Ibrāhīm from Abī al-Ḥasan عليه السلام: “She is entitled to the blood-money.”

key_terms.ٱلدِّيَةُ: financial compensation prescribed for killing or bodily injury
key_terms.ٱلْجَنِينُ: the fetus, for which staged blood-money assessments are given
key_terms.ٱلْعَثْمُ: deformity or faulty healing after a fracture
key_terms.ٱلْقَسَامَةُ: oath-based evidentiary procedure used in injury and homicide cases
key_terms.ٱلْمَعْقُولَةُ: collective indemnity liability borne by the responsible side
key_terms.ٱلْمُوضِحَةُ: a wound that exposes the bone

ai.seo_question: What are the blood-money rulings for bodily injuries, fractures, and fetal harm in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith records an extensive legal register of blood-money, bodily injury assessments, fractures, wounds, fetal injury, and evidentiary procedures attributed to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام and affirmed by the Imams عليهم السلام. It is a jurisprudential text concerned with precise judicial rulings, proportional compensation, qasāmah, and administrative implementation in cases of physical harm.
